sections.title: Storm Damage Identification - Hail & Wind
sections.content:
**Becoming a Storm Damage Expert**

**The $47,000 Hail Hit Marcus Almost Missed**

Marcus had been knocking doors for three weeks when he climbed onto the Thompson family's roof on a sunny Tuesday morning. The homeowner, Linda Thompson, stood in her driveway looking skeptical. "I've had four other roofers up there," she called up. "They all said there's nothing wrong."

Marcus felt his stomach drop. Four other roofers? Maybe there really wasn't any damage. But he remembered his Team Leader's words: "When in doubt, sign it up. Not every roof will look destroyed by 2-inch hail, but we still find a lot of success."

As Marcus scanned the shingles, he almost missed them. The impacts weren't dramatic - no obvious craters or gaping holes. But when he got down on his knees and looked closely with his flashlight, there they were: dozens of circular divots, each about the size of a quarter. The granules had been knocked away, exposing the black asphalt mat underneath. Some showed slight bruising around the impact points.

"Linda," Marcus called down, "can you come take a look at these photos?"

Fifteen minutes later, Linda signed the Contingency Agreement. The insurance adjuster arrived three days later and approved a full replacement: $47,000. Linda called Marcus that evening, her voice emotional. "Those other four roofers walked right over this damage. Thank God you took the time to really look."

Marcus learned something critical that day: **Storm damage identification is a skill that separates amateurs from professionals.** The damage is often there - you just have to train your eyes to see it.

---

**Your ability to identify and document storm damage determines your success.** Master these identification techniques to find qualifying damage on every roof.

**Hail Damage Recognition:**

[PHOTO:tag=hail]

**Primary Indicators:**
- **Circular divots** - Round impact marks on shingles where hailstones struck
- **Granule loss** - Black asphalt mat showing through protective granules
- **Bruising** - Darkened areas where impact compressed shingle material
- **Soft spots** - Areas that feel soft when pressed gently (use caution)

**Visual Cues:**
- Look for pattern of circular impacts across multiple slopes
- Check all slopes - damage is rarely isolated to one area
- Use flashlight to enhance visibility of subtle damage
- Granules collect in gutters and downspouts (smoking gun evidence)

**Pro Tip from the Field:**
> "I carry a high-powered flashlight even on sunny days. The angle of light can reveal hail divots that are nearly invisible to the naked eye. This one tool has helped me find damage on 'clean' roofs dozens of times." - Jason K., Top 5% Producer

**Wind Damage Identification:**

[PHOTO:tag=wind]

**Primary Indicators:**
- **Creased shingles** - Folded or bent shingles where wind lifted and bent them back
- **Blown-off shingles** - Missing shingles or exposed sections
- **Lifted tabs** - Shingle tabs no longer sealed down, vulnerable to further damage
- **Torn shingles** - Ripped or damaged sections from wind force

**Wind Damage Story:**

When Elena inspected the Martinez property after the April windstorm, the damage was obvious from the ground - three shingles were missing entirely from the front slope. But when she got on the roof, she found something more: dozens of creased shingles on the back slope where wind had lifted and folded them. "The missing shingles got me on the roof," Elena later told her team, "but the creased shingles got them a $52,000 claim approval. Always check all slopes, not just the obvious damage."

**Collateral Damage Documentation:**

[PHOTO:tag=collateral]

Collateral damage builds your case with insurance adjusters. The more evidence you document, the stronger the claim.

- **Gutters** - Dents from hail impacts (highly visible, hard to dispute)
- **Downspouts** - Visible dents or damage along length
- **Screens** - Holes or tears from hail penetration
- **Siding** - Impact marks or damage on vinyl/aluminum
- **Roof metals** - Flashing, vents, pipes with visible damage

**Critical Principle:**
> "WHEN IN DOUBT, SIGN IT UP. Not every roof will look destroyed by 2-inch hail, but we still find a lot of success. Your job is to document thoroughly, present confidently, and let the insurance adjuster make the final determination. Err on the side of giving homeowners the opportunity to file a claim."

sections.title: 15-20 Minute Inspection Protocol
sections.content:
**Professional Inspection Sequence**

**Devon's Landscape Photo Disaster**

Devon had been with RoofER for two months when he made a costly mistake. He completed a thorough inspection on the Patterson property, found qualifying hail damage, helped file the claim, and secured the Contingency Agreement. Everything seemed perfect.

Three days later, his Team Leader called. "Devon, we have a problem. The Photo Report for Patterson won't populate correctly. Did you take photos in landscape?"

Devon's heart sank. He had. "I thought landscape captured more of the roof," he explained.

"I understand," his Team Leader said patiently, "but the system requires portrait orientation. Landscape photos won't process. You'll need to go back and re-shoot everything."

Devon returned to the Patterson home that evening, embarrassed, and re-took all 47 photos in portrait orientation. Mr. Patterson was gracious but confused. "Didn't you just do this?"

Lesson learned: **Portrait orientation, always. No exceptions.** Devon never made that mistake again.

---

Execute this exact sequence on every inspection for consistency, efficiency, and complete documentation.

**Pre-Inspection (2 minutes):**
- Confirm homeowner permission ("I'm heading up now!")
- Verify insurance company ("Who do you have insurance with?")
- Set expectations ("This will take about 10-15 minutes")
- Ensure ladder safety (check stability, proper angle)

**Photo Sequence (Required Order - PORTRAIT ORIENTATION ONLY):**

**1. Mailbox/House Number Photo**
- Establishes property identity for insurance claim
- First photo of every inspection, no exceptions
- Clearly shows address or house number

**2. Overview of House**
- Full house shot from street
- Shows overall property condition and context
- Helps adjuster locate property during scheduling

**3-6. Elevation Collateral Damage (Front, Right, Rear, Left)**

For EACH elevation, photograph in this order:
- **Screen damage** (holes, tears from hail)
- **Gutter damage** (dents, detachment)
- **Downspout damage** (dents, bends)
- **Siding damage** (cracks, impacts)

**Why All Four Elevations Matter:**
Collateral damage on multiple elevations proves the storm was severe and widespread. Insurance adjusters cannot dismiss multi-elevation damage as pre-existing or isolated incidents.

**7. Roof Overview Collateral**
- Roof metal damage (flashing, vents, pipes)
- Other roof collateral damage
- Wide shot showing overall roof condition

**8. Circle Hail Hits (4-6 Close-Ups Per Slope)**
- Close-up of EACH hail impact
- Use chalk to circle damage clearly
- Minimum 4-6 close-ups per slope (more if extensive damage)
- Get close enough that impact details are visible

**Chalk Circle Technique:**
Circle should be large enough to see from 3-4 feet away but not so large it obscures the damage. Circle around the divot, not over it. Multiple circles in one photo show pattern of impacts.

**9. Slash Wind Damage (As Applicable)**
- Close-up of EACH wind-damaged shingle
- Use chalk to slash mark (differentiates from hail circles)
- Document creases, missing shingles, lifted tabs

**10. Overview of Chalked Damage**
- Wide shot showing marked damage across roof
- Proves damage pattern, not isolated incidents
- Should show multiple circles/slashes visible from distance

**11. Granules in Gutters/Downspouts**
- Photo of granule accumulation in gutters
- Close-up showing quantity and concentration
- Evidence of shingle deterioration from hail impacts

**The Granules Story:**

When Priya showed Mrs. Chen the photos from her inspection, Mrs. Chen was skeptical. "Those look like normal wear marks to me," she said.

Priya pulled up the last photo - granules packed into the gutter. "Mrs. Chen, these granules are what protect your shingles from UV damage and water penetration. When hail knocks them off - as you can see here - your shingles lose their protective layer. This level of granule loss doesn't happen from normal aging. This is impact damage."

Mrs. Chen leaned closer. "I never thought about where those black specks in my gutters came from."

Priya smiled. "Most people don't. That's why we show you. This is evidence your insurance company will take very seriously."

Mrs. Chen signed the agreement that afternoon. Claim approved two weeks later: $38,500.

---

**Safety Reminder:**
- **If unsafe, DO NOT DO THE INSPECTION**
- Wet roofs, steep pitches, damaged structures = safety hazard
- Document from ground if necessary
- Use drone photos if available
- Escalate to Team Leader for guidance

**Your safety is more important than any sign-up.**

sections.title: Post-Inspection Pitch - Presenting Your Findings
sections.content:
**Turning Damage into Action: The Art of Presenting Findings**

**James and the Skeptical Engineer**

James descended the ladder at the Patel residence, his iPad full of hail damage photos. Mr. Patel, a structural engineer, stood waiting with arms crossed. "So? What's the verdict?"

James had been warned by other reps: engineers are the toughest homeowners. They want data, explanations, and proof.

"Mr. Patel, thank you for your patience. I found significant hail damage across multiple slopes. Let me walk you through the photos so you can see exactly what I documented."

James started with the mailbox photo, then the house overview. Mr. Patel nodded. "Logical sequencing. Go on."

As James progressed through the elevation collateral photos, Mr. Patel's expression shifted from skepticism to interest. "These gutter dents are consistent with hail impact patterns."

"Exactly," James said. "Now let me show you the roof damage itself." He displayed the circled hail impacts. "See these circular divots? When hail strikes a shingle, it creates this characteristic impact pattern. The divot fills with water, which freezes in winter and expands, breaking down the shingle integrity through repeated freeze-thaw cycles."

Mr. Patel took the iPad, zooming in. "This is clear impact damage. The granule displacement and underlying mat exposure are textbook hail indicators."

James then showed the granule accumulation in gutters. "And this is what I call the smoking gun."

Mr. Patel looked up. "How soon can we file the claim?"

Fifteen minutes later, the claim was filed and agreements were signed. As James packed up, Mr. Patel shook his hand. "You presented that like a professional engineer. Well done."

James walked to his car with a smile. Even skeptical engineers become believers when you present evidence methodically and explain the science behind the damage.

---

The Post-Inspection Pitch is your moment to transform roof damage into a committed homeowner. Master this presentation to convert inspections into signed agreements and filed claims on the same day.

## **Photo Presentation Sequence**

**Opening Statement:**
"Thank you for your patience while I completed the inspection. Let me walk you through what I found on your roof. I'm going to show you these photos in the order I took them so you can see exactly what I documented."

**1. Start with the Mailbox/House Number Photo**
- "This confirms we're documenting the right property"
- Establishes professionalism and organization

**2. Overview of House**
- "This is the overall view of your home from the street"
- Sets context for inspection

**3. Elevation Collateral Damage (All Four Sides)**

For each elevation (Front, Right, Rear, Left), present evidence:

**Screen Damage:**
- "These screens have multiple impact points from hail. You can see the holes here and here."

**Gutter Damage:**
- "Notice these dents in your gutters - these are classic hail impact signatures."

**Downspout Damage:**
- "Your downspouts show significant hail damage as well."

**Siding Damage:**
- "The siding has taken impacts on multiple elevations."

**Why Collateral Matters:**
> "All of this collateral damage is evidence that builds your case with the insurance company. It proves the storm was severe enough to damage multiple surfaces, not just isolated spots."

**4. Roof Collateral - Metals, Flashing, Vents, Pipes**
- "When metal surfaces like these vents show impact damage, it confirms hail struck your roof with force."

**5. Circled Hail Damage - The Main Event**

**Introduction:**
"Now let me show you the actual damage to your shingles. I've circled each hail impact so you can clearly see what I'm documenting."

**For Each Hail Damage Photo:**

**Visual Description:**
- "See this circular divot? That's where a hailstone struck your roof."
- "Notice the exposed black mat where granules have been knocked off."

**Functional Impact Explanation:**
> "Here's what happens with hail damage: When hail strikes a shingle, it creates these divots. Those divots fill with water. In winter, that water freezes and expands. The freeze-thaw cycle breaks down the shingle integrity over time. Eventually, these damaged shingles will crack and fail, leading to leaks inside your home."

**Granule Loss Explanation:**
> "The granules on your shingles serve two critical functions: they protect the underlying mat from UV damage, and they provide the waterproofing layer. When hail knocks off these granules - as you can see in these photos - it exposes the black asphalt mat underneath. Without that granule protection, your shingles deteriorate much faster than their rated lifespan. Even though your roof might be 10, 15, or 20 years old, the hail damage has compromised its ability to protect your home for the remaining years it was designed to last."

**Multiple Slopes Evidence:**
"As you can see, this damage is not isolated to one area. I found hail impacts across multiple slopes of your roof, which is exactly what insurance companies need to see to approve a full replacement."

**6. Slashed Wind Damage (If Applicable)**

**Creased Shingles:**
- "These shingles have been creased by wind. Once a shingle is creased, it loses its seal and becomes vulnerable to blow-off and water infiltration."

**Blown-Off Shingles:**
- "Here you can see where shingles have been completely blown off, exposing the underlayment."

**7. Overview of Chalked Damage**
- "This overview photo shows the pattern of damage across your entire roof. Insurance adjusters need to see that this is not just one or two isolated hits - this is widespread storm damage."

**8. Granules in Gutters/Downspouts - The Smoking Gun**
- "Finally, here's what I call the smoking gun evidence. Look at all these granules collected in your gutters and downspouts. These are the protective granules that have been knocked off your shingles by hail. This level of granule loss significantly reduces your roof's remaining lifespan."

---

## **Positioning RoofER as the Homeowner's Advocate**

After presenting all photos:

**Expert Positioning:**
> "As storm damage experts, we see this all the time. Insurance companies are in the business of minimizing payouts, not maximizing what you're entitled to under your policy. That's where we come in. We document everything thoroughly, we know exactly what to present to the adjuster, and we make sure you get a fair shake. Our job is to be your advocate through this entire process."

**Reassurance:**
> "I know this can feel overwhelming, but here's the good news: if your insurance company fully approves your claim - which based on this damage, they should - your only out-of-pocket cost is your deductible. Everything else is covered by your insurance policy that you've been paying for all these years."

---

## **Handling Common Homeowner Questions**

**"How bad is this damage really?"**
- "The damage I documented meets the threshold for insurance approval. The functional impact is clear - these damaged shingles will not protect your home for their intended lifespan."

**"Do I really need a full replacement?"**
- "Insurance companies and manufacturers require full slope replacements when damage is found. You can't just patch a few shingles - that would void your warranty and leave you with mismatched materials."

**"What if insurance denies the claim?"**
- "That's exactly why we document everything so thoroughly. If there's any pushback, we have templates, building codes, and manufacturer guidelines to support your claim. We'll be with you every step of the way."

**"What's my next step?"**
- "Let's file your claim today while we're here together. I have the Claim Filing Information Sheet right here. It takes about 10 minutes. Then we'll get you signed up with a Contingency Agreement that protects you."

---

## **The Transition to Claim Filing**

**Smooth Bridge:**
"Based on everything I've shown you, you have qualifying storm damage that should be covered by your insurance policy. The next step is to file a claim with your insurance company. I can help you do that right now - it only takes about 10 minutes. Do you know who your insurance carrier is?"

**If they hesitate:**
"I completely understand if you want to think about it. However, here's why I recommend filing today: insurance companies have strict timelines for storm damage claims. The sooner we file, the sooner we can get an adjuster out here, and the sooner you can get your roof protected properly. Plus, I've already done all the hard work of documenting the damage. All we need to do now is submit this evidence to your carrier."

**Assumptive Close:**
"Let's go ahead and get this filed. Do you have your insurance app on your phone, or do you prefer to call them directly?"

---

**Key Success Principles:**

1. **Confidence is Contagious** - Speak with authority about the damage
2. **Education Over Pressure** - Explain WHY damage matters
3. **Visual Evidence is Powerful** - Let photos do most of the talking
4. **Same-Day Commitment** - File claim and sign agreements before you leave

sections.title: Claim Filing & Documentation Mastery
sections.content:
**From Inspection to Filed Claim: Same-Day Excellence**

**Natalie's First Same-Day Filing**

Natalie had completed her third inspection of the day at the Rodriguez residence. She'd found qualifying hail damage, presented the photos confidently, and Mrs. Rodriguez seemed convinced.

"So what do I do now?" Mrs. Rodriguez asked.

"We file your insurance claim right now, while I'm here," Natalie said, pulling up the Claim Filing Information Sheet on her iPad. "It takes about 10 minutes."

Mrs. Rodriguez hesitated. "Can I think about it overnight?"

Natalie remembered her training: momentum fades fast. "I completely understand. But here's what I've learned: when homeowners wait overnight, they start overthinking. They talk to their neighbor who had a bad experience five years ago, or they Google 'filing insurance claims' and get overwhelmed. Then they never call back. But you have qualifying damage that should be covered. Let's just get it filed today."

Mrs. Rodriguez nodded slowly. "Okay. Let's do it."

Twenty minutes later, the claim was filed, agreements were signed, and Natalie had documented everything in the Field Portal. As she drove to her next appointment, her Team Leader texted: "Great work on Rodriguez! This is how you build momentum."

Natalie learned something crucial that day: **Same-day filing is the difference between a sign-up and a lost lead.**

---

Mastering the claim filing process is critical to your success. The goal is simple: file every claim on the same day as the inspection while everything is fresh and momentum is high.

## **Understanding the Claim Filing Process**

You are not filing on the homeowner's behalf - you are guiding them through filing their own claim with your expert assistance.

### **Three Filing Methods**

**Method 1: Insurance App (Preferred)**
- Most modern carriers have mobile apps
- Fastest and most convenient
- Immediate confirmation and claim number
- Photo upload capability built-in

**Method 2: Insurance Website (Alternative)**
- Login to carrier website on homeowner's phone or laptop
- Online claim filing portal
- Similar to app experience

**Method 3: Phone Call to Insurance (Backup)**
- Call insurance claims department
- Walk through claim details verbally
- Claim number issued over phone

**Priority Order:**
> Always ask for app or website login FIRST. Only use phone method if homeowner doesn't have app access or website login credentials.

---

## **The Claim Filing Information Sheet**

Your essential tool for capturing all necessary information.

**Information You Will Collect:**

**1. Homeowner Details**
- Full legal name (as appears on policy)
- Property address and mailing address
- Phone number and email
- Date of birth (sometimes required)

**2. Insurance Policy Information**
- Insurance carrier name
- Policy number
- Policy effective dates
- Deductible amount

**3. Storm Information**
- Date of storm (specific date if known)
- Type of storm (hail, wind, both)
- Hail size and wind speed (if reported)

**4. Damage Description**
- Primary damage: Roof
- Secondary damage: Gutters, downspouts, screens, siding
- When homeowner first noticed damage

**5. Access Information**
- Gate codes (if applicable)
- Dog on property (safety for adjuster)
- Best days/times for adjuster meeting

---

## **Step-by-Step Claim Filing Walkthrough**

**Phase 1: Pre-Filing Preparation (5 minutes)**
- Sit down with homeowner at table or kitchen
- Have homeowner get insurance card/policy documents
- Set expectations: "This will take about 10 minutes"

**Phase 2: Information Collection (5 minutes)**
- Fill out Claim Filing Information Sheet systematically
- Ask for policy number, carrier, deductible
- Reference known storm dates in your area

**Phase 3: Claim Submission (Using App/Website)**

**Step 1: Access the Platform**
"Do you have your [Insurance Company] app on your phone? Great! Let's open it up and go to the claims section."

**Step 2: Navigate to Claims Filing**
- Look for "File a Claim" button
- Select "Property Claim" or "Homeowner Claim"
- Choose "Storm Damage" or "Weather-Related Damage"

**Step 3: Enter Claim Details**

**Description of Damage (Dictate):**
> "Storm damage to roof, gutters, downspouts, and screens. Hail damage visible on shingles including circular divots, granule loss, and exposed mat. Wind damage including creased and lifted shingles. Collateral damage to gutters, downspouts, and window screens. Professional roofing contractor (RoofER) has documented damage with photos and recommends full inspection by insurance adjuster."

**Step 4: Request Adjuster Inspection**
- **SELECT YES** - Always request in-person adjuster inspection

**Step 5: Request Adjuster Contact You**

In notes/comments, add:
> "Homeowner requests adjuster contact RoofER sales representative [YOUR NAME] at [YOUR PHONE] to schedule inspection meeting."

**Why This Matters:** You maintain control of scheduling and ensure you're present at adjuster meeting.

**Step 6: Review and Submit**
- Review all information for accuracy
- Homeowner clicks "Submit Claim"
- **Screenshot or write down CLAIM NUMBER immediately**

---

## **Common Objections During Claim Filing**

**"Will this raise my insurance rates?"**
- "Filing a claim for storm damage - which is a covered peril - should not raise your rates. Storm damage is what homeowner's insurance is designed for."

**"I need to talk to my spouse first."**
- "I totally understand. However, since I've already documented everything, and the process is just 10 minutes, would it make sense to at least get the claim filed today? Your spouse can still be involved in every step."

**"What if insurance denies it?"**
- "That's exactly why we document so thoroughly. If there's any pushback, we have templates, building codes, and manufacturer guidelines to support your claim. Also, remember - the Contingency Agreement is null and void if not fully approved. You risk nothing by filing."

---

## **Same-Day Documentation Requirements**

**Immediately After Claim Filed:**

1. **Update Field Portal App:**
   - Move job to "Claim Filed" stage
   - Enter claim number in notes
   - Set follow-up reminder (2 days out)

2. **Upload Photos to Field Portal:**
   - All photos in correct sequence
   - Portrait orientation only
   - Organized by category

3. **GroupMe Announcement:**
   - Post sign-up to team GroupMe
   - Format: "Sign up / Roof / Gutters / Screens / [Insurance] / [Last Name]"

**NEVER DELAY DOCUMENTATION**

**Critical Rule:**
> Document same day as inspection. If you discover missing photos, return to property immediately. Never let documentation slip to tomorrow.

agnesContent.title: Safety First, Always
agnesContent.content: Before we dive into inspection techniques, let's talk about something critical: your safety. I've seen too many eager reps rush onto dangerous roofs because they didn't want to lose a potential sign-up. Please hear me on this - no commission is worth getting hurt.
points: Wet roofs are slip hazards. If it rained recently, wait until dry or document from ground. Your Team Leader would rather you come back tomorrow than risk a fall today.
Steep pitches (above 8/12) require extra caution. If you're uncomfortable, trust your gut. Use drone photography or escalate to an experienced climber.
Always check ladder stability before climbing. Three-point contact rule: two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand on ladder at all times.
Worn shoes = danger. Invest in quality roofing shoes with good grip. Replace them when treads wear down.
If you feel unsafe at any point, come down. Document from ground level. Your safety matters more than any deal.

agnesContent.title: Photo Documentation: Your Insurance Evidence Package
agnesContent.content: Your photos are not just documentation - they're your legal evidence package that will determine whether a claim gets approved or denied. I've seen perfect inspections lose claims because of poor photo quality. Let's make sure that never happens to you.
points: ALWAYS portrait orientation. I cannot stress this enough. Landscape photos will not populate in the Photo Report Template. You'll have to go back and reshoot everything. Learn from others' mistakes.
Chalk circles should be large enough to see from 3-4 feet away, but not so large they obscure the actual damage. Circle around the divot, not over it.
Lighting matters enormously. Use your flashlight even on sunny days to create contrast. Angled light reveals divots that are invisible in flat lighting.
Minimum 4-6 close-ups per slope for hail damage. More is better. Insurance adjusters want to see pattern of damage, not just one or two impacts.
Granules in gutters photo is your smoking gun. Get close enough to show the quantity and concentration. This single photo has saved countless claims from denial.
Every photo should be clear, focused, and properly exposed. Blurry photos raise red flags with adjusters. Take your time. Reshoot if needed.

agnesContent.title: Training Your Eye to See Storm Damage
agnesContent.content: Here's something nobody tells new reps: storm damage identification is a learned skill. Your first 20 roofs will be confusing. You'll second-guess everything. That's normal. By roof 100, you'll spot damage in seconds. Let me share what separates beginners from experts.
points: Hail damage is often subtle. Not every impact will be a dramatic crater. Look for circular patterns, slight depressions, and granule displacement. Get down on your knees and look closely.
Use your hand to feel for soft spots. Gently press around suspected impact areas. Damaged shingles often feel softer than undamaged ones. (Be careful not to create new damage.)
Check ALL slopes, not just the most visible ones. I've seen reps miss qualifying damage because they only checked the front slope. Storms don't discriminate by slope direction.
Collateral damage validates roof damage. If gutters, screens, and siding show impacts, the roof almost certainly has damage too. Use collateral as confirmation.
When in doubt, sign it up. Let the adjuster make the final call. Your job is to give homeowners the opportunity to file a claim. Their insurance company will determine approval.
Keep a photo library of confirmed hail damage on your phone. Compare suspected damage to your reference photos. This trains your eye over time.

agnesContent.title: Presenting Your Findings Like a Pro
agnesContent.content: The Post-Inspection Pitch is where you transition from friendly door-knocker to trusted expert. Homeowners are looking to you for guidance. Your confidence (or lack of it) will determine whether they trust your assessment. Here's how to nail this critical moment.
points: Start with collateral damage photos, not roof damage. This builds credibility. When homeowners see their gutters and screens damaged, they become receptive to hearing about roof damage.
Explain the WHY behind damage, not just the WHAT. Don't just say 'this is hail damage.' Explain the freeze-thaw cycle. Explain granule loss and UV exposure. Education builds trust.
Use the phrase 'smoking gun' when showing granules in gutters. This creates a moment of realization for homeowners. They understand granule loss in a visceral way.
Pause after showing key photos. Let evidence sink in. Don't rush through presentation. Silence is powerful - it lets homeowners process what they're seeing.
Position yourself as their advocate against insurance companies. Frame the relationship as: You + Homeowner vs. Insurance Company. You're on their team.
Transition to claim filing confidently. Don't ask 'Do you want to file a claim?' Say 'Let's get this claim filed today.' Assumptive language creates forward momentum.

agnesContent.title: Same-Day Filing: Your Path to High Conversion
agnesContent.content: Here's a hard truth: 80% of homeowners who say 'let me think about it overnight' never file. The moment you leave, doubt creeps in. They talk to skeptical neighbors, Google horror stories, or just forget. Same-day filing is non-negotiable for top performers. Let me show you how to make it effortless.
points: File the claim BEFORE presenting agreements. This order matters. Once claim is filed, momentum carries into agreement signing. If you ask for agreements first, homeowners get nervous.
Use the app or website method whenever possible. Phone calls take longer, involve hold times, and give homeowners time to reconsider. Digital filing is fast and creates instant commitment.
Have the Claim Filing Information Sheet printed or digital. Fill it out as you walk through with homeowner. This shows professionalism and keeps process moving.
Request adjuster contact YOU directly in claim notes. This is critical. If adjuster contacts homeowner first, you lose control of the timeline and might miss the meeting.
Screenshot the claim number immediately. Text it to homeowner. This creates sense of completion and progress. Homeowners feel accomplished and are ready to sign agreements.

If homeowner resists same-day filing, address the real objection. Usually it's not about timing - it's about fear of commitment or insurance premium concerns. Use LEARN Framework to uncover and address real concern.

agnesContent.title: Documentation Discipline Wins Deals
agnesContent.content: I'm going to be blunt: reps who slack on documentation lose deals and commissions. I've seen it happen dozens of times. Adjuster shows up, photo report is incomplete, claim gets denied or reduced. Don't let this be you. Documentation discipline is what separates top 10% performers from everyone else.
points: Upload photos to Field Portal THE SAME DAY as inspection. Not tomorrow. Not next week. Same day. Set a rule: don't leave the field until photos are uploaded.
Update job status in Field Portal immediately after claim filing. Move to 'Claim Filed' stage, add claim number, add adjuster contact when assigned.
Post sign-ups to GroupMe right away. This isn't just celebration - it's accountability. Your team knows you filed the claim and will follow up if you don't close the deal.
Keep Claim Filing Information Sheet for every job. You'll need this info for adjuster meeting prep. Store it in Field Portal notes or take photo of completed sheet.
If you discover missing photos after leaving property, GO BACK. Yes, it's annoying. Yes, it's embarrassing. But it's better than losing a claim approval because you're missing critical evidence.

Create end-of-day documentation routine: (1) Upload all photos, (2) Update Field Portal, (3) Post GroupMe sign-ups, (4) Set reminders for adjuster follow-ups. This 15-minute routine protects your pipeline.

interactiveLearning.title: Storm Damage Identification Simulator
interactiveLearning.content: Test your ability to identify hail damage, wind damage, and collateral damage from realistic roof photos

activities.title: Hail Damage vs. Age-Related Wear
activities.description: Distinguish between hail damage and normal aging

data.scenario: You see circular indentations with exposed black mat on a 15-year-old roof. Homeowner says 'isn't this just old age?' What do you say?
options: You're right, this is probably just aging. Let me check other areas.
This is hail damage. The circular pattern and granule displacement are classic hail indicators. Age-related wear appears more uniform across the entire roof.
It's hard to tell the difference. You should probably call a more experienced inspector.
It could be either. Let's file a claim and let the adjuster decide.
feedback: Never dismiss potential damage without investigation. This response gives up too easily.
Correct! Educate homeowner on the difference: hail creates circular patterns with granule displacement, while age-related wear is uniform. This builds your credibility.
This undermines your authority. You are the expert. Homeowners need you to be confident in your assessment.
While letting adjuster decide is sometimes right, you should still provide educated assessment based on visual evidence.

activities.title: Understanding Collateral Damage Value
activities.description: Learn why collateral damage strengthens claims

data.scenario: You find hail damage on the roof but no visible collateral damage on gutters or screens. How does this affect your approach?
options: This is a problem. Without collateral damage, the claim will likely be denied.
Collateral damage helps but isn't required. Document roof damage thoroughly and proceed with claim filing.
Skip this property. Claims without collateral damage never get approved.
Tell the homeowner their damage isn't qualifying without collateral evidence.
feedback: Collateral damage strengthens claims but is not required for approval. Roof damage can stand alone if well-documented.
Correct! Collateral damage builds your case, but roof damage can be sufficient. Document what you find thoroughly and file the claim. Let the adjuster make the final determination.
This is too extreme. Many claims get approved based solely on roof damage. Never pre-reject a potential claim.
This discourages homeowners unnecessarily. Your job is to give them the opportunity to file, not to pre-judge claim viability.

activities.title: Identifying Wind Damage Correctly
activities.description: Recognize different types of wind damage

data.scenario: You see shingles with distinct fold lines and creases. No shingles are missing. What type of damage is this and how severe?
options: This is minor cosmetic damage, not worth filing a claim
This is qualifying wind damage. Creased shingles lose their seal and become vulnerable to water infiltration and further damage.
This is installation error, not storm damage
This is thermal damage from heat, not wind
feedback: Creased shingles are qualifying wind damage, not cosmetic. This response undervalues legitimate damage.
Correct! Creased shingles are qualifying wind damage. Once a shingle is creased, it loses its seal and becomes vulnerable. This is a valid insurance claim.
While poor installation can cause issues, distinct fold lines and creases are typically from wind uplift, not installation error.
Thermal damage presents differently than wind creasing. Wind creates distinct fold lines at shingle edges.

activities.title: Understanding Granule Loss
activities.description: Explain the significance of granule loss to homeowners

data.scenario: Homeowner asks: 'What's the big deal about these little black specks in my gutters? Isn't that normal?'
correctPoints: Explain granules protect shingles from UV damage
Explain hail knocks off granules, exposing asphalt mat
Explain accelerated deterioration without granule protection
data.sampleResponse: Those 'little black specks' are actually the protective granules from your shingles. Granules serve two critical functions: they protect the underlying mat from UV damage, and they provide your waterproofing layer. When hail knocks off these granules - as we're seeing here - it exposes the asphalt mat underneath. Without that granule protection, your shingles deteriorate much faster than their rated lifespan. This is what I call smoking gun evidence of hail damage. It's not normal wear - it's impact damage.

activities.title: Applying 'When In Doubt, Sign It Up'
activities.description: Practice decision-making for borderline damage scenarios

data.scenario: You're on a roof and you see what might be hail damage, but it's subtle - just slight depressions and minor granule loss. You're not 100% certain. What do you do?
options: Tell homeowner there's no qualifying damage and move to next door
Document thoroughly, present findings, and file claim. Let the adjuster make final determination.
Call your Team Leader for a second opinion before presenting anything
Tell homeowner you think there might be damage but you're not sure
feedback: This violates the 'When in doubt, sign it up' principle. You're pre-rejecting potential claims that might be valid.

Correct! 'When in doubt, sign it up.' Document thoroughly, present with confidence, and let the insurance adjuster make the final determination. Your job is to give homeowners the opportunity to file claims, not to pre-judge approval likelihood.

While seeking guidance is good for learning, you should be empowered to document and present borderline cases. Call Team Leader if truly unsafe or unusual, but don't delay sign-ups waiting for approval.
This undermines your authority and credibility. Present your findings confidently. If there's damage, present it as damage. If adjuster disagrees later, that's their job.

interactiveLearning.title: Post-Inspection Pitch Role-Play
interactiveLearning.content: Practice delivering Post-Inspection Pitch to different homeowner personalities

activities.title: The Skeptical Homeowner
activities.description: Homeowner is doubtful about damage severity

data.scenario: You present hail damage photos. Homeowner says: 'That doesn't look that bad to me. Are you sure this needs to be replaced?'
correctApproach: Use granule loss as smoking gun evidence
Position as advocate against insurance denials
data.sampleResponse: I understand how it might not look dramatic from these photos. The thing about hail damage is that the functional impact happens over time, not immediately. These divots fill with water, which freezes in winter and expands, breaking down shingle integrity. Insurance companies and manufacturers require full slope replacement when this type of damage is found - you can't just patch a few shingles without voiding warranties. That's why this granule loss in your gutters is so significant. Your shingles are losing their protective layer. As your advocate, my job is to make sure your insurance company covers what they're supposed to cover under your policy.

data.scenario: Homeowner is an engineer. After showing photos, they ask: 'What's the actual mechanism of failure here? How does this compromise structural integrity?'
correctApproach: Discuss granule composition and UV protection
data.sampleResponse: Great question. The failure mechanism is multi-stage. First, hail impact creates divots that compromise the shingle's surface integrity. These divots collect water. During freeze-thaw cycles, water expands by approximately 9%, creating micro-fractures in the asphalt mat. Over repeated cycles, these fractures propagate, leading to mat failure. Simultaneously, granule displacement exposes the asphalt mat to direct UV radiation. Granules contain ceramic-coated minerals that reflect UV and protect the underlying petroleum-based asphalt. Without granule protection, UV degradation accelerates dramatically, reducing the effective lifespan by 40-60% according to manufacturer testing. The combination of mechanical fracturing and accelerated UV degradation creates a failure timeline of 3-7 years post-impact, depending on climate conditions.

data.scenario: As soon as you start showing damage photos, homeowner interrupts: 'Stop right there. I can't afford a new roof. We don't have that kind of money.'
correctApproach: Explain only cost is deductible (if approved)
Position as actually saving them money
data.sampleResponse: I completely understand your concern - roofing is a major expense. But here's the great news: if your insurance company approves this claim, your only out-of-pocket cost is your deductible. Everything else is covered by your insurance policy that you've been paying into for years. This is exactly what homeowner's insurance is designed for - storm damage coverage. Let me show you the rest of the damage I found, and then we'll file the claim together. If insurance fully approves it, you're just paying your deductible. If they don't fully approve it, our Contingency Agreement is null and void - you owe us nothing. Fair enough? Let me show you what I found.

activities.title: Homeowner Doesn't Have App
activities.description: Handle situation when app is not available

data.scenario: Homeowner doesn't have insurance app and doesn't remember website password. What's your best approach?
options: Tell them to download app now and reset password
Ask if they can reset password via email quickly, or switch to phone call method
Leave and ask them to file claim themselves later
File claim yourself using their information
feedback: Downloading app and resetting password takes time and breaks momentum. Phone call is faster backup.
Correct! Quick password reset is fine if it takes 2-3 minutes. Otherwise, switch to phone call method to maintain momentum and ensure same-day filing.
Never leave without filing. Same-day filing is critical. Use phone method if digital not available.
You cannot file claim on behalf of homeowner. They must be the one to submit claim. Your role is to guide and assist.

activities.title: Handling 'I Need to Talk to Spouse' During Filing

data.scenario: You're about to file claim when homeowner says: 'Actually, I should probably talk to my husband first before filing anything.'
correctApproach: Clarify that spouse can be involved in every step
Emphasize claim filing is just reporting damage
Offer to speak with spouse now (phone call)
data.sampleResponse: I totally understand wanting to include your husband in this decision. Here's the thing - filing the claim is just reporting that damage exists. It doesn't commit you to anything yet. That's what the Contingency Agreement is for, which we'll review after filing. Your husband will be CC'd on all communications with insurance, and we'll make sure he's present for the adjuster meeting. The reason I recommend filing today is that insurance companies have strict timelines for storm damage claims. The sooner we file, the sooner we get an adjuster out here. Is your husband available for a quick phone call right now? I'm happy to explain everything to him.

activities.title: Build a Professional Photo Report
activities.description: Drag and drop the photo report steps into the correct sequence.

items.text: Label and upload to Field Portal

quiz.question: What orientation MUST you use when taking inspection photos for Photo Reports?
options: Landscape - captures wider view
Portrait - landscape will not populate properly in templates
Either orientation works fine
Landscape for overviews, portrait for close-ups
quiz.explanation: Photo Reports MUST be in portrait orientation. Landscape photos will not populate properly in the Photo Report Template and will cause processing delays. This is non-negotiable. You'll have to return to property and reshoot if you take landscape photos.

quiz.question: What are the first TWO photos you take on every inspection?
options: Roof overview and hail damage close-ups
Mailbox/House number and Overview of house from street
Front elevation and roof access point
Insurance documents and homeowner ID
quiz.explanation: Every inspection starts with (1) Mailbox/House Number to establish property identity, then (2) Overview of House from the street to show overall context. This sequence is required for all claims.

quiz.question: How do you mark hail damage vs wind damage on the roof with chalk?
options: Hail = X marks, Wind = Circle marks
Hail = Circle marks, Wind = Slash marks
Hail = Red chalk, Wind = Blue chalk
Both types use the same marking system
quiz.explanation: Hail damage is CIRCLED with chalk, Wind damage is SLASHED with chalk. This helps insurance adjusters quickly identify damage types when they arrive for inspection. Consistent marking is professional and clear.

quiz.question: What are the THREE primary indicators of hail damage?
options: Cracks, holes, and missing shingles
Circular divots, granule loss, and bruising
Fading, curling, and blistering
Moss growth, algae stains, and discoloration
quiz.explanation: The three primary indicators of hail damage are: (1) Circular divots where hailstones struck, (2) Granule loss exposing the black asphalt mat, and (3) Bruising (darkened areas from impact compression). These distinguish hail damage from age-related wear or other damage types.

quiz.question: Why is granule loss from hail damage a serious concern?
options: It makes shingles look ugly but doesn't affect function
Granules protect shingles from UV damage and provide waterproofing. Without them, shingles deteriorate much faster.
Granule loss only matters on very old roofs
It voids the manufacturer warranty but doesn't cause actual damage
quiz.explanation: Granules serve two critical functions: they protect the underlying asphalt mat from UV damage, and they provide the waterproofing layer. When hail knocks off granules, it exposes the mat to accelerated deterioration, significantly reducing the roof's effective lifespan. This is functional damage, not just cosmetic.

quiz.question: Why is documenting collateral damage (gutters, screens, siding) important for insurance claims?
options: It increases the claim payout amount
It proves the storm was severe and widespread, making roof damage harder to dispute
It's required by law for all storm damage claims
It allows you to sell additional services
quiz.explanation: Collateral damage on gutters, screens, and siding proves the storm was severe enough to damage multiple surfaces, not just isolated spots. This makes it harder for insurance adjusters to dismiss roof damage as pre-existing or age-related. It builds your case with corroborating evidence.

quiz.question: When explaining hail damage to homeowners, what is the freeze-thaw cycle and why does it matter?
options: It's when shingles get cold and brittle in winter, making them more likely to crack
Hail divots fill with water. In winter, water freezes and expands, breaking down shingle integrity over time.
It's the natural aging process of shingles through seasonal temperature changes
It's when ice dams form and damage shingles from underneath
quiz.explanation: The freeze-thaw cycle explanation is critical for homeowners: Hail impact creates divots. These divots fill with water. In winter, that water freezes and expands. The expansion creates micro-fractures in the shingle. Over repeated freeze-thaw cycles, these fractures propagate and the shingle fails. This explains WHY hail damage matters, not just WHAT it looks like.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary indicator of wind damage?
options: Creased shingles (folded or bent)
Blown-off shingles (missing sections)
Circular divots with granule loss
Lifted tabs (shingle tabs unsealed)
quiz.explanation: Circular divots with granule loss are indicators of HAIL damage, not wind damage. Wind damage appears as creased shingles, blown-off sections, lifted tabs, or torn shingles. Understanding the difference helps you accurately identify and mark damage types.

quiz.question: Complete this critical principle: 'WHEN IN DOUBT, _______.'
options: Call your Team Leader for approval
Sign it up - let the adjuster decide
Tell the homeowner you're not sure
Skip the property and move to next door
quiz.explanation: WHEN IN DOUBT, SIGN IT UP. Not every roof will look destroyed, but we still find a lot of success. Your job is to document thoroughly, present confidently, and let the insurance adjuster make the final determination. Err on the side of giving homeowners the opportunity to file a claim.

quiz.question: What is the 'smoking gun' evidence for hail damage claims?
options: Missing shingles on the front slope
Granules accumulated in gutters and downspouts
Homeowner testimony about hearing hail
Weather reports showing hail in the area
quiz.explanation: Granules accumulated in gutters and downspouts are the 'smoking gun' evidence. This shows that protective granules have been knocked off shingles by impact, proving damage occurred. It's visual, undeniable evidence that even skeptical homeowners understand immediately.

quiz.question: What is the best opening statement for the Post-Inspection Pitch?
options: "Bad news - your roof is damaged and needs replacement."
"Thank you for your patience. Let me walk you through what I found, starting with these photos in the order I took them."
"I found some damage, but I'm not sure if it's enough for a claim."
"You're definitely going to need a new roof. Let me show you why."
quiz.explanation: The best opening is professional, organized, and neutral: 'Thank you for your patience. Let me walk you through what I found, starting with these photos in the order I took them.' This sets up a methodical presentation and positions you as a professional expert, not a pushy salesperson.

quiz.question: When should you file the insurance claim with the homeowner?
options: Within 24-48 hours after the inspection
Same day as the inspection, before leaving the property
After they've had time to think it over (next day)
After the Contingency Agreement is signed
quiz.explanation: File the claim SAME DAY as inspection, BEFORE leaving the property. Momentum fades fast. Homeowners who 'think it over' rarely follow through. Same-day filing = high conversion rate. File claim first, then secure agreements while momentum is high.

quiz.question: What is the PREFERRED method for filing insurance claims?
options: Phone call to insurance company
Mailing a written claim form
Insurance company app or website
Email to insurance agent
quiz.explanation: Insurance app or website is preferred. It's fast, convenient, provides immediate claim number, and maintains momentum. Only use phone call as backup if homeowner doesn't have app access or website login. Digital methods create instant commitment.

quiz.question: When filing a claim, what CRITICAL request should you make regarding the adjuster?
options: Request expedited scheduling within 24 hours
Request adjuster contact you (the rep) directly to schedule inspection meeting
Request the most experienced adjuster
Request virtual inspection instead of in-person
quiz.explanation: CRITICAL: Request adjuster contact YOU directly to schedule the inspection meeting. This ensures you're present, you control the timeline, and you can avoid scheduling conflicts. Add this in claim notes/comments: 'Homeowner requests adjuster contact RoofER rep [YOUR NAME] at [YOUR PHONE].'

quiz.question: What is the correct GroupMe format for announcing a sign-up?
options: "Got another one! Roof job in [neighborhood]"
"Sign up / Roof / Gutters / State Farm / Johnson"
"Claim filed for [address] - roof and gutters"
"New sign-up: [customer name], [insurance company]"
quiz.explanation: Correct format: 'Sign up / Storm Damage Item 1 / Item 2 / Insurance Company / Customer Last Name'. Example: 'Sign up / Roof / Gutters / State Farm / Johnson'. This standardized format allows team to quickly track sign-ups and maintain consistent communication.
